title: Women and Economics

It is a prose work of 1898 by Charlotte Perkins Gilman; it belongs to The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
plot_or_argument: Gilman argues that women are the only class in history maintained entirely by another class; that this dependency distorts both sexes and the home; and that women must be given access to productive work and to economic independence, with the domestic functions socialised and professionalised.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
literary_form: Sociological treatise; review essay
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
historical_context: 1898: the American suffrage campaign, the new women's colleges and professions, and the evolutionary sociology of Lester Ward. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within The New Woman and the Fin-de-Siècle Problem Novel; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Women and Economics is the founding American work of feminist economics and one of the most influential feminist books ever written: it was translated into seven languages, made Gilman an international figure, and its analysis of unpaid domestic labour anticipates the whole modern discussion.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Perkins Stetson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Small, Maynard in Boston in November 1898. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Herland
description: Published in the Forerunner in 1915 and the first sustained American feminist utopia: the discovery of a country inhabited entirely by women and the consequences for three male explorers. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by Charlotte Perkins Gilman; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
plot_or_argument: Three American men find Herland, a country without men where the women reproduce parthenogenetically, have built a harmonious civilisation of gardens and education, and have no war, poverty or crime; the three men marry Herland women, and the novel ends with Terry's expulsion after he tries to force himself on his wife Alima, Jeff staying behind with the pregnant Celis, and the narrator, Van, leaving with his wife Ellador to show her the outside world.
narrative_structure: It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: Vandyck Jennings (Van), the narrator; Terry O. Nicholson; Jeff Margrave; Ellador; Alima; Celis; Somel; Zava; Moadine
literary_form: Utopian novel (serialised in the Forerunner, 1915)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
historical_context: The 1910s: the American suffrage movement, the First World War, and the utopian tradition of Bellamy and Morris. The record dates the work as composed between 1914 and 1915 and first published in 1915 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: Herland is the founding American feminist utopia and the most influential work of its kind before the 1970s: its vision of a society organised by women has shaped feminist science fiction from Marge Piercy to Ursula Le Guin.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charlotte Perkins Stetson. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in The Forerunner, the author's own monthly, from July to December 1915 and first published in book form by Pantheon Books in New York in 1979. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture
alternative_titles: Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture
description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's most ambitious work of cultural criticism: an analysis of how the whole of American culture — art, religion, education, law and language — has been shaped by male dominance.
plot_or_argument: Gilman examines the 'androcentric' bias in literature, art, dress, cookery, medicine, education and government, and argues that human culture has been distorted by the exclusion of half of humanity and that the correction of this bias is the great task of the modern age.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
literary_form: Cultural criticism; review essay
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
historical_context: 1910: the suffrage campaign, the new sociology of gender, and the American Progressive era. The record dates the work as composed in 1910 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The Man-Made World is a founding text of feminist cultural criticism and one of the first systematic analyses of what would later be called the social construction of gender.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1911, as cultural criticism, by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. Composed in 1910. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Moving the Mountain
description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's first utopia: the return of an American who has been lost for thirty years to a country transformed by feminism and social reform. It is a prose fiction work of 1911 by Charlotte Perkins Gilman; it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation.
plot_or_argument: John Robertson, presumed dead, returns to America in 1940 to find a country without poverty, with professionalised housework and childcare, communal kitchens, a rational education and full equality for women, and he is gradually converted to the new order.
narrative_structure: A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: John Robertson (the narrator); his sister Nellie (Ellen), now a university president; the citizens of the transformed America of 1940
literary_form: Utopian novel; early scientific romance
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is clear, argumentative prose in the service of a thesis.
historical_context: The 1910s: the Progressive era and the American utopian tradition of Bellamy's Looking Backward. The record dates the work as composed between 1910 and 1911 and first published in 1911 and it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation.
literary_significance: Moving the Mountain is one of the founding American feminist utopias and the most detailed picture of Gilman's social programme; it is a key text in the history of American utopian fiction and of the Progressive movement.

title: Up from Slavery
description: Published in 1901 and one of the great American autobiographies: the account of a life from slavery in Virginia to the founding of Tuskegee Institute. It is a prose work of 1901 by Booker T. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Washington describes his childhood in slavery, his work in the salt and coal mines, his years at Hampton Institute, and the building of Tuskegee from a borrowed room to a great institution, and ends with his advice to the black youth of America.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
principal_characters: Booker T. Washington, the narrator; his mother; Mrs Viola Ruffner; General Samuel C. Armstrong, of Hampton; Olivia Davidson
literary_form: Autobiography; review essay, first issued in 1901
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of struggle and institutional building.
historical_context: The 1856-1901: slavery and emancipation, Reconstruction, and the rise of the 'Tuskegee machine' in black American politics. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Up from Slavery is the central African-American autobiography of the post-Reconstruction era and one of the classic American narratives of self-making: it made Washington the most powerful black man in America and defined the politics of uplift for a generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Booker Taliaferro Washington. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: The chapters ran in The Outlook from 1900 and the book was published by Doubleday, Page in New York in March 1901 and by Chatto and Windus in London the same year. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: 'The Atlanta Exposition Address'
description: Delivered at Atlanta on 18 September 1895 and the most consequential African-American speech of the century: the address in which Washington accepted social segregation in exchange for economic opportunity.
plot_or_argument: Washington tells the white audience that 'in all things purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress', and calls on black Americans to cast down their buckets where they are and to make themselves indispensable through labour and education.
narrative_structure: The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery. An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review.
literary_form: Oration (Atlanta Cotton States and International Exposition)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the platform: the spoken sentence, the repetition and the triadic climax, the direct address to the audience, the apostrophe and the peroration, printed as delivered. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of struggle and institutional building.
historical_context: 1895: the Plessy v. Ferguson decision of the following year, the collapse of Reconstruction, and the rise of Jim Crow. The record dates the work as composed in 1895 and first published in 1895 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under lecture and popular address; review essay and quarterly argument.
literary_significance: The Atlanta address is the founding document of the accommodationist strategy in American race politics and one of the most debated speeches in American history: it made Washington the leader of black America, and it set the terms of the argument that Du Bois would answer in The Souls of Black Folk.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Booker Taliaferro Washington. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1895, by Booker T. Washington. Composed in 1895. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Future of the American Negro
description: Published in 1899 and Washington's fullest statement of his social philosophy: a series of essays on the past, present and future of black Americans. It is a prose work of 1899 by Booker T. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address.
plot_or_argument: Washington argues that the negro has advanced more in thirty years than any other race in history, that industrial education and the ownership of property are the true foundations of citizenship, and that the South's prosperity depends on the progress of its black population.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
literary_form: Essays and addresses; review essay
meter_and_prosody: Prose. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of struggle and institutional building.

The record dates the work as composed in 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: The Future of the American Negro is the central statement of Washington's programme and a key text in the history of American race relations: it shows the strengths and the costs of the strategy of accommodation at the moment of its greatest power.

title: The Story of My Life and Work
alternative_titles: Story of My Life and Work

plot_or_argument: Washington tells the story of his birth in slavery, his education at Hampton, the founding of Tuskegee, and his public career, in a version written for a subscription audience and filled with the details of the institution's growth.

literary_form: Autobiography (first version)

The record dates the work as composed between 1899 and 1900 and first published in 1900 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; novel of development and the growth story.

title: Working with the Hands
description: Published in 1904 and Washington's fullest account of the Tuskegee method: a book on the dignity of manual labour and the teaching of trades. It is a prose work of 1904 by Booker T. Washington; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.
plot_or_argument: Washington describes the teaching of agriculture, carpentry, brickmaking, dressmaking and housekeeping at Tuskegee, and argues that the education of the hand is the education of the whole person and the foundation of black economic independence.

A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
literary_form: Essays on industrial education
meter_and_prosody: Prose. The author's characteristic manner is first-person narrative of struggle and institutional building.
historical_context: The 1900s: the industrial education movement, the Tuskegee curriculum, and the American debate on vocational training. The record dates the work as composed between 1903 and 1904 and first published in 1904 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.

title: The Conjure Woman
description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's first collection: seven stories told by the old freedman Uncle Julius, in which the conjure tales of slavery turn the plantation tradition against itself. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; Ghost Story and Scientific Supernatural Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Uncle Julius tells the northern narrator and his wife about the conjure woman Aunt Peggy and her spells — 'The Goophered Grapevine', 'Po' Sandy', 'Mars Jeems's Nightmare', 'The Conjurer's Revenge', 'Sis' Becky's Pickaninny' — and each tale records the cruelty of slavery under cover of a comic anecdote.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A short narrative in which the witness's account is given first, the strange event is approached by stages, and the explanation is withheld at the close.
principal_characters: Uncle Julius McAdoo; John, the Ohio narrator; Annie, his wife; Aunt Peggy, the conjure woman; Mars Dugal' McAdoo; Henry ('The Goophered Grapevine'); Sandy and Tenie ('Po' Sandy'); Mars Jeems McLean
literary_form: Collection of seven linked stories
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.
historical_context: The 1890s: the North Carolina plantation country, the American plantation tradition of Harris and Page, and the market for dialect fiction. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
literary_significance: The Conjure Woman is the founding work of African-American fiction and a permanent rebuke to the plantation tradition: its frame narrative turns the minstrel tale into a record of slavery's cruelty, and it is one of the most important books in the history of American race and literature.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charles Waddell Chesnutt. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston in March 1899, with the introduction by William Dean Howells. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Marrow of Tradition
description: Published in 1901 and the central American novel of the Wilmington coup of 1898: a fictional account of the white supremacist massacre that destroyed black political power in North Carolina. It is a prose fiction work of 1901 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Sensation Novel; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The novel interweaves the lives of two families — the white Carters and the black Millers, who are half-sisters — with the political campaign that culminates in the burning of the black newspaper office and the massacre of the black citizens of Wellington.
narrative_structure: A novel of sensation in chapters, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, testimony and documents inserted into the narrative, each part closing on a cliff.
principal_characters: Dr Adam Miller; Janet Miller; Major Carteret; Olivia Carteret; Jerry; Josh Green; Captain McBane; General Belmont; Sandy Campbell; Ellis
literary_form: Novel; sensation novel, first issued in 1901
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of sensation: the cliff-edge chapter ending, the first-person testimony and the document inserted into the narrative, the secret withheld and revealed by stages, and the vocabulary of the law, the asylum and the will. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.
historical_context: 1898: the Wilmington coup and massacre, the white supremacy campaigns of the 1890s, and the collapse of black political rights in the South. The record dates the work as composed between 1900 and 1901 and first published in 1901 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program; Local Colour and the Regionalist School, it is catalogued under sensation novel; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: The Marrow of Tradition is the first American novel about the Wilmington massacre and the most important American novel of white supremacist terror: it is the founding text of the African-American political novel and a permanent historical record of a massacre that American history tried to forget.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Charles Waddell Chesnutt. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: The Wife of His Youth and Other Stories of the Color Line
alternative_titles: Wife of His Youth and Other Stories of the Color Line
description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's second collection: stories of the colour line in the post-Reconstruction North and South, including the famous title story. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Charles W. Chesnutt; it belongs to Local Colour and the Regionalist School and it is catalogued here under Local-Colour Sketch and the Regional Portrait; New Woman and Marriage-Question Novel.
plot_or_argument: In 'The Wife of His Youth', Mr Ryder, a light-skinned leader of a society of mixed-race people, is asked to acknowledge the old black wife he married in slavery; he does so, and the story ends with his public recognition of her. Other stories include 'Her Virginia Mammy', 'The Sheriff's Children' and 'A Matter of Principle'.
narrative_structure: A short framed narrative or descriptive set piece, the dialect transcribed and the place named exactly. A novel in chapters built on the marriage question: the courtship, the settlement, the discovery of the terms, and the decision.
principal_characters: Mr Ryder and 'Liza Jane ('The Wife of His Youth'); Sheriff Campbell and Tom, the mulatto prisoner ('The Sheriff's Children'); Clara Hohlfelder and John Winthrop ('Her Virginia Mammy'); Cicero and Alice Clayton ('A Matter of Principle'); Grandison and Dick Owens ('The Passing of Grandison'); Ben Davis ('The Web of Circumstance')
literary_form: Collection of nine stories; local-colour sketch
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the local-colour sketch: the transcribed dialect, the exact naming of places, trades, foods and weather, and the short framed narrative or descriptive set piece. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is frame narrative that turns the oral tale against itself.

The record dates the work as composed between 1888 and 1899 and first published in 1899 and the corpus places it within Local Colour and the Regionalist School; American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under local-colour sketch and the regional portrait; new woman and marriage-question novel.
